title: Hadhramaut
capsule: The ancient kingdom of Hadhramaut (Ḥaḍramawt in South Arabian script) was one of the four main pre-Islamic South Arabian states occupying the Hadhramaut valley and the Dhofar coastal corridor in what is now eastern Yemen and western Oman, with its capital at Shabwa. Attested in Sabaean and Minaean inscriptions from at least the 8th century BCE, Hadhramaut competed and occasionally allied with Saba, Ma'in, and Qataban over control of the frankincense and myrrh trade routes to the Mediterranean. The kingdom faded from epigraphic record by the early 4th century CE, likely absorbed into the expanding Himyarite realm that unified most of southern Arabia before the Islamic conquest.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The kingdom's existence and capital at Shabwa are firmly attested epigraphically, but its territorial extent—particularly the precise boundary with Qataban to the west and Dhofar to the east—is reconstructed from inscriptions and remains poorly constrained.
